summary: Defines the Extensible Binary Meta Language (EBML), a binary container format designed for audio and video storage, like a binary counterpart to XML. It uses nested elements with identifiers, lengths and values, and describes EBML Schemas, similar to XML Schemas. Matroska builds on it.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of nesting boxes where each box has a label and a size. It packs video and sound compactly.

questions: what file formats are built on ebml
what is a variable-size integer in ebml
how does ebml relate to matroska
subtitle: A compact binary format for nested, self-describing data, built to store audio and video.

tldr.problem: Multimedia container formats need a generic, space-efficient, easy-to-parse way to nest data, with structure kept separate from meaning.
tldr.mechanism: Every EBML Element is an Element ID, an Element Data Size and Element Data. IDs and sizes are variable-size integers that say their own length, and an EBML Schema defines which elements a document type may contain.
tldr.outcome: EBML is the structural layer used by the Matroska container. The RFC defines the header, element types, versioning, CRC-32 and Void elements, and IANA registries. A later RFC updates it.

facts.label: Default max Element Data Size length

today: RFC 8794 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 9559, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What EBML Is
sections.content:
EBML (Extensible Binary Meta Language) is a binary format aligned with octets and inspired by XML. The goal is a generic, binary, space-efficient format that can define more complex formats using an EBML Schema. The RFC says EBML is used by the multimedia container Matroska, and that other uses are out of scope.

Like HTML and XML, it separates structure from semantics. Apart from the EBML Header and a few Global Elements, the RFC defines no particular semantics. Formats such as Matroska and WebM define their own on top.

The building block is the Element, made of three parts: an Element ID (the tag), an Element Data Size (the length) and Element Data (the value). Elements can nest, which makes the approach easy to parse and allows selective parsing.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a toy box where every item has a name tag and a size label. You can open the boxes you care about and skip the others.

sections.title: Variable-Size Integers, IDs and Sizes
sections.content:
Element IDs and Element Data Sizes are both encoded as a Variable-Size Integer (VINT). A VINT is a VINT_WIDTH of zero or more 0 bits, a single 1 bit called the VINT_MARKER, then VINT_DATA. The number of zero bits plus the marker gives the length in octets. A one-octet VINT has 7 data bits, a two-octet one has 14, a three-octet one has 21. The data is a big-endian unsigned integer. The same value may be written at longer lengths, for example the integer 2 as 0x82 or 0x4002, so a field can be overwritten later.

Element IDs are one to four octets by default (longer if EBMLMaxIDLength says so). The data bits MUST NOT be all zeros or all ones, and the ID MUST use the shortest valid length.

Element Data Sizes are one to eight octets by default and need not be shortest. All-zero data means an Empty Element. All-one data is reserved for unknown size, allowed only for Master Elements whose schema permits it. An eight-octet size can express 2^(56)-2 octets, about 72 petabytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The first few zero bits at the start of a number tell you how many bytes long the number is, like a note that says how many pages follow.

sections.title: Element Types and Documents
sections.content:
Every element in a schema has one of eight types: Signed Integer, Unsigned Integer, Float, String, UTF-8, Date, Master and Binary. Integers, floats and dates are stored big-endian. Integers can be zero to eight octets long, floats zero, four or eight octets (IEEE 754), and a String holds printable ASCII (0x20 to 0x7E). A Date is a signed integer counting nanoseconds from 2001-01-01T00:00:00 UTC. A Master Element contains other elements, and a Binary Element is not interpreted by the reader.

An EBML Document is an EBML Header followed by an EBML Body, and MUST NOT contain data outside elements. An EBML Stream is a file of one or more concatenated documents, each starting with a new header at the root level.

The header is a Master Element named EBML with ID 0x1A45DFA3. It holds EBMLVersion, EBMLReadVersion, EBMLMaxIDLength (default 4), EBMLMaxSizeLength (default 8), DocType, DocTypeVersion, DocTypeReadVersion and optional DocTypeExtension elements. The DocType names the schema, such as Matroska or WebM.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only a few kinds of boxes: whole numbers, decimals, plain text, dates, boxes that hold other boxes, and boxes of raw stuff nobody opens.

sections.title: EBML Schemas
sections.content:
An EBML Schema is a well-formed XML document that defines the elements of one document type, the way an XML Schema relates to an XML document. Its top-level element is EBMLSchema, in the namespace urn:ietf:rfc:8794, and it needs a docType and a version. One schema documents all versions of a document type, using minver and maxver to say when elements appear or are deprecated.

Each element has a name, a path, an ID and a type. The path gives the full hierarchy with backslashes. A schema MUST declare exactly one Root Element, and MUST NOT use ID 0x1A45DFA3, which is reserved for the header so a reader can resynchronize. Root and Top-Level Element IDs SHOULD be at least four octets long.

Two Global Elements can appear in any parent. CRC-32 (ID 0xBF) holds a 32-bit checksum of its parent's data and, if present, MUST be the parent's first element. Void (ID 0xEC) is discarded and reserves space or overwrites data.
sections.plainLanguage: A schema is the rulebook that says which boxes may go inside which, and what each label means.

sections.title: Editing, Versions and Compatibility
sections.content:
Two version pairs govern reading: EBMLVersion and EBMLReadVersion for the header, and DocTypeVersion and DocTypeReadVersion for the body. A reader that supports at least the ReadVersion can read the document.

The RFC also describes how to edit a document without rewriting it. To shrink an element by one octet, rewrite the Element Data Size one octet longer. For more than one octet, fill the gap with a Void Element. Terminating a String or UTF-8 value with null octets is allowed but NOT RECOMMENDED. If a parent has a CRC-32, it MUST be verified before the change and updated afterwards.

For evolution, new mandatory elements need defaults that match the earlier state. Non-mandatory elements can be added in a new DocTypeVersion, and deprecated ones SHOULD be discarded when found in newer documents.
sections.plainLanguage: If a label gets shorter, you can pad the leftover space instead of moving every other box.

sections.title: Security and Registries
sections.content:
EBML itself offers no confidentiality or authorization, and only marginal integrity through CRC elements. Even if the content layer encrypts, the DocType and the element structure can leak information.

The RFC lists hostile inputs a reader may reject: invalid sizes that run past the parent, huge lengths meant to cause out-of-memory conditions, invalid UTF-8 or dates, missing mandatory elements and CRC mismatches. It also warns about side channels such as padded values that look different but mean the same, stray data inside a Master Element, and Void Elements used to hide content.

IANA gets two new registries: EBML Element IDs, for elements that can occur in the header (including Global Elements), and EBML DocTypes. One-octet IDs fall between 0x81 and 0xFE and are allocated by the RFC Required policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The boxes are not locked. A careful reader checks that sizes make sense so a tricky file cannot fool it.
